title: 23 — Observability & Performance
html:
23 — Observability & Performance

Monitoring answers questions you knew to ask. Observability lets you answer questions you didn't. The difference matters at 03:00 when the failure is one you've never seen before.

1. The three signals (plus the two people forget)

Signal Answers Cost Cardinality
Metrics Is something wrong? Aggregated numbers over time Cheap, constant ⚠️ Must be low
Logs What exactly happened? Discrete events with detail Expensive at volume Unlimited
Traces Where did the time go, across services? Moderate (sampled) High
Profiles Which code consumed the CPU/memory? Moderate (continuous profiling) —
Events/changes What did we change just before it broke? Trivial —

⚠️ The last one is chronically neglected and is the highest-value signal in an incident. Overlay deployments, config changes, and feature-flag flips on every dashboard. The answer to "what changed?" resolves a large share of incidents in the first five minutes.

flowchart LR
    A[Alert fires — an SLO is at risk] --> B[Metrics: what is degraded,<br/>and how widely?]
    B --> C[Change events: what shipped<br/>in the last hour?]
    C --> D[Traces: which service/operation<br/>owns the latency or errors?]
    D --> E[Logs for that trace id:<br/>the exact failure]
    E --> F[Profile / dump if it's<br/>CPU or memory]

This ladder is the whole discipline. Design your telemetry so you can walk it without leaving your tooling or guessing.

2. Structured logging

// ❌ A string. Unqueryable, unaggregatable, and it interpolates even when the level is disabled.
logger.LogInformation($"Rebalanced portfolio {id} with {count} trades in {ms}ms");

// ✔ A structured event with named, typed, queryable fields.
logger.LogInformation(
    "Portfolio rebalanced {PortfolioId} {TradeCount} {ElapsedMs}",
    portfolioId, tradeCount, elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);

// ✔ Scopes attach context to everything logged inside them
using (logger.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object>
{
    ["CorrelationId"] = correlationId,
    ["TenantId"]      = tenantId,
    ["UserId"]        = userId,
}))
{
    await ProcessAsync(ct);      // every log inside carries these fields
}

With structured logs you can ask PortfolioId == 42 AND ElapsedMs > 1000 across billions of entries. With string logs you can grep, badly.

2.1 Levels — and what each one commits you to

Level Meaning Action
Trace/Debug Developer detail Off in production (or sampled/dynamically enabled)
Information A significant business event happened Normal. Keep the volume deliberate
Warning Something unexpected but handled; may need attention Reviewed, not paged
Error An operation failed; a user or a job is affected Should be actionable — investigate every one
Critical The system or a subsystem is down Page someone

⚠️ If nobody acts on your Errors, the level is wrong. Log-level inflation ("everything is an Error") destroys the signal — the team stops looking, and then a real error hides among 40,000 handled ones.

2.2 Rules

Do Don't
One event per meaningful operation, with its outcome and duration Log entry and exit for every method
Include the correlation/trace id in every entry Rely on timestamps to correlate
Log the exception object (logger.LogError(ex, ...)) — you get the stack trace LogError(ex.Message) — you lose the stack and the inner exception
Log decisions and their inputs (why the branch was taken) Log the entire request/response body
Sample high-volume, low-value events Log inside tight loops
Redact PII and secrets at the source Assume "it's an internal log"
Use consistent field names across services (UserId, not userId/user_id/uid) Ad-hoc naming — it makes cross-service queries impossible

Cost control: logging is often the largest observability bill. Sample Information on high-traffic paths, keep Error/Warning at 100%, set retention by class (7 days hot, 90 days archived), and review the top 10 log sources by volume quarterly — there's always one chatty line producing 60% of the data.

3. Metrics

3.1 Types

Type Use Example
Counter Monotonically increasing http_requests_total, orders_created_total
Gauge A value that goes up and down queue_depth, active_connections, memory_bytes
Histogram Distribution → percentiles http_request_duration_seconds
Summary Client-computed quantiles Rarely the right choice — histograms aggregate correctly, summaries don't

⚠️ Never alert on averages. An average latency of 200 ms is compatible with 5% of users waiting 4 seconds. p95 and p99 are what users experience; the average is what nobody experiences.

⚠️ Cardinality is the thing that will break your metrics system. Every unique combination of label values is a separate time series. A user_id label on a service with 1M users creates 1M series and will take down Prometheus (and your bill). Labels must be low-cardinality and bounded: endpoint (templated, not the raw URL), method, status class, region, tenant tier — never IDs, never raw paths, never error messages.

3.2 What to measure

RED — for every request-driven service:

  • Rate: requests per second
  • Errors: failed requests per second (and as a ratio)
  • Duration: latency distribution

USE — for every resource:

  • Utilisation: % busy
  • Saturation: queue depth / waiting work
  • Errors: error count

Four Golden Signals (Google SRE): latency, traffic, errors, saturation — RED + saturation.

And the ones that actually matter to the business: orders placed, reports generated, logins, revenue per minute. A business metric detects outages that infrastructure metrics miss — "everything is green but nobody has placed an order in 20 minutes" is the alert you want.

// .NET built-in metrics API (OpenTelemetry-compatible)
public sealed class OverlapMetrics
{
    private readonly Counter<long> _computed;
    private readonly Histogram<double> _duration;
    private readonly UpDownCounter<long> _inFlight;

    public OverlapMetrics(IMeterFactory factory)
    {
        var meter  = factory.Create("Shop.Overlap");
        _computed  = meter.CreateCounter<long>("overlap.computed", unit: "{report}");
        _duration  = meter.CreateHistogram<double>("overlap.duration", unit: "ms");
        _inFlight  = meter.CreateUpDownCounter<long>("overlap.in_flight");
    }

    public void Recorded(double ms, string outcome, string tenantTier) // BOUNDED label values only
    {
        _computed.Add(1, new("outcome", outcome), new("tier", tenantTier));
        _duration.Record(ms, new("outcome", outcome));
    }
}

4. Distributed tracing

Trace (one user request, one trace id)
├── span: POST /api/rebalance                       [420 ms]
│   ├── span: authorise                             [  3 ms]
│   ├── span: SELECT portfolio + holdings           [ 45 ms]
│   ├── span: HTTP GET pricing-service/quotes       [180 ms]  ← the cost
│   │   └── span: (in pricing) SELECT prices        [160 ms]  ← the real cost
│   ├── span: compute trades                        [ 30 ms]
│   └── span: INSERT trades + outbox                [ 40 ms]

W3C Trace Context (traceparent header) propagates the trace and parent span ids across services. Most instrumentation libraries handle it automatically for HTTP; you must propagate it manually across message queues (file 14 §9) — otherwise the trace stops at the async boundary, which is exactly where you most need it.

builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry()
    .ConfigureResource(r => r.AddService(serviceName: "overlap-api", serviceVersion: version))
    .WithTracing(t => t
        .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation(o => o.RecordException = true)
        .AddHttpClientInstrumentation()
        .AddSqlClientInstrumentation(o => o.SetDbStatementForText = true)   // ⚠️ check for PII in SQL
        .AddSource("Shop.Overlap")
        .SetSampler(new ParentBasedSampler(new TraceIdRatioBasedSampler(0.1)))
        .AddOtlpExporter())
    .WithMetrics(m => m
        .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation()
        .AddRuntimeInstrumentation()
        .AddMeter("Shop.Overlap")
        .AddOtlpExporter());

// Custom spans for business operations
using var activity = ActivitySource.StartActivity("ComputeOverlap");
activity?.SetTag("portfolio.count", portfolios.Count);
activity?.SetTag("as_of", asOf.ToString("O"));

Sampling: head-based (decide at the start — simple, but you may discard the interesting traces) vs tail-based (decide after completion — keep all errors and all slow traces, sample the rest). Tail-based is what you want; it needs a collector that buffers spans. A pragmatic default: 100% of errors and slow requests, 1–10% of the rest.

OpenTelemetry is the answer to vendor lock-in: instrument once with OTel, export to Jaeger/Tempo/Application Insights/Datadog/Honeycomb by changing configuration.

5. Correlation — the thing that ties it together

One id must flow through every log line, span, message, and error response for a request.

app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    var correlationId = context.Request.Headers["X-Correlation-Id"].FirstOrDefault()
                        ?? Activity.Current?.TraceId.ToString()
                        ?? Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N");

    context.Response.Headers["X-Correlation-Id"] = correlationId;   // return it to the client
    Activity.Current?.SetTag("correlation_id", correlationId);

    using (logger.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object> { ["CorrelationId"] = correlationId }))
        await next();
});

Surface it to users in error pages and API error bodies. A support ticket that says "reference 4bf92f35" turns a two-hour investigation into one query.

6. SLIs, SLOs, and alerting

6.1 Definitions (recap from file 02 §7)

  • SLI — a measurement: proportion of requests that succeed in under 300 ms.
  • SLO — the target: 99.9% over 30 days.
  • Error budget — 1 − SLO: 43 minutes of failure per month, spendable.

6.2 Alert on symptoms, not causes

❌ Alert on ✔ Alert on
CPU > 80% User-facing error rate > SLO burn rate
Memory > 90% p99 latency above the SLO
A pod restarted Requests failing / queue age growing
Disk 70% full Disk will be full in 4 hours (predictive)

Why: high CPU with users unaffected is not an incident. Users failing with normal CPU is. Cause-based alerts produce noise and train people to ignore pages.

6.3 Multi-window burn-rate alerting

Alerting on "error rate > 1% for 5 minutes" is either too noisy or too slow. Burn rate fixes it:

Burn rate = how fast you're consuming the error budget relative to the sustainable rate. Burn rate 1 = exactly on budget for the period; burn rate 14.4 = the entire monthly budget in ~2 days.

Severity Condition Response
Page 14.4× burn over 1 h and over 5 min Wake someone — the budget is gone in 2 days
Page 6× burn over 6 h and over 30 min Urgent
Ticket 3× burn over 24 h Investigate next working day
Ticket 1× burn over 3 days Track the trend

The two-window requirement (long window for significance, short window for currency) prevents both false alarms and alerts that fire long after the problem resolved.

6.4 Alert hygiene

Every alert must have: a clear title naming the user impact, a runbook link, an owner, and a severity that maps to a defined response. Anything that doesn't require action within the response time is a dashboard item or a ticket, not a page.

⚠️ Alert fatigue is a reliability risk, not an annoyance. Track pages per on-call shift. More than ~2 actionable pages per shift means the system or the alerting needs work; a shift full of non-actionable pages means real ones will be missed. Delete or downgrade any alert that has been ignored three times.

7. Dashboards that work in an incident

Three tiers:

  1. Service overview (one screen per service): RED metrics, error budget remaining, saturation, dependency health, deployment markers.
  2. Business overview: the handful of numbers the company cares about, so a broken funnel is visible even when infrastructure looks healthy.
  3. Deep-dive: per-endpoint, per-dependency, per-queue — reached from the overview, not memorised.

Design rules: the top-left panel answers "is this service healthy?" in two seconds; everything shows the same time range; percentiles not averages; annotate deploys and incidents; a link to the runbook on the dashboard itself.

8. Performance engineering

8.1 The method

flowchart LR
    A[Define the target<br/>p99 < 300 ms at 500 rps] --> B[Measure the current state]
    B --> C[Find the bottleneck<br/>— profile, don't guess]
    C --> D[Fix ONE thing]
    D --> E[Measure again]
    E --> F{Target met?}
    F -->|No| C
    F -->|Yes| G[Add a regression guard<br/>load test in CI]

Amdahl's law applies to optimisation effort too: optimising something that accounts for 5% of the time yields at most a 5% improvement. Always attack the largest contributor first, and re-profile after each change because the bottleneck moves.

8.2 Latency arithmetic

  • Serial dependencies add. Six sequential 50 ms calls = 300 ms. Parallelise the independent ones.
  • Tail latency dominates fan-out. If one call has a 1% chance of taking 1 second, a request that makes 100 such calls has a 63% chance of hitting at least one. This is why p99 of a component becomes the p50 of a fan-out request — and why hedged requests and aggressive timeouts exist.
  • Queueing theory: as utilisation → 100%, wait time → ∞. At 80% utilisation the average wait is roughly 4× the service time; at 90% it's 9×. Never plan capacity above ~70% steady-state utilisation — the last 20% of headroom buys you nearly all of your latency stability.

8.3 The usual bottlenecks, in the order you should check them

Rank Cause Detection Fix
1 Database — missing index, N+1, table scan, lock waits Trace shows DB spans dominating; slow-query log File 10 §3, §6
2 Chatty network calls Many small spans in the trace Batch, cache, colocate, parallelise
3 Blocking / thread-pool starvation High latency, low CPU, growing queue length File 12 §2.4
4 Payload size Large response bytes; slow TTLB but fast TTFB Projection, pagination, compression
5 Serialisation CPU profile shows JSON work Source-generated serialisers, smaller DTOs
6 GC pressure High allocation rate, time-in-GC > 10% File 16 §2.4
7 Cold start / JIT First requests slow after deploy Warm-up, R2R, keep-alive, pre-provisioned instances
8 Lock contention High CPU or low CPU with low throughput Reduce critical sections, partition state
9 Algorithmic Cost grows superlinearly with input Files 03–04

8.4 Profiling

Question Tool (.NET) Tool (other)
Where is CPU spent? dotnet-trace + PerfView/Speedscope, Visual Studio profiler perf, py-spy, Chrome DevTools
What is allocating? dotnet-counters, dotnet-gcdump, VS allocation profiler memray, heap snapshots
Why is it hanging? dotnet-dump + parallel stacks jstack, py-spy dump
Which query is slow? Query Store, pg_stat_statements —
Frontend? Chrome Performance panel, Lighthouse, Angular DevTools —
Always-on in production Continuous profiling (Pyroscope, Datadog, App Insights Profiler) —

Continuous profiling is underrated: it answers "why was the service slow at 02:14 last Tuesday?" without reproducing the problem.

8.5 Load testing

Test before you need to, at 2× expected peak, against a production-shaped environment with production-shaped data volumes. Key outputs: the throughput ceiling, the latency curve as load increases, the failure mode past the ceiling, and the resource that saturates first.

⚠️ A load test against a 1,000-row database tells you nothing. Data volume changes query plans; that's often the entire difference between test and production.

9. Frontend observability

Backend telemetry misses what users experience. Add: Core Web Vitals (LCP < 2.5 s, INP < 200 ms, CLS < 0.1), JS error tracking with source maps, API call latency as seen by the browser (includes DNS, TLS, and network), route-change timing, and real-user monitoring segmented by device and geography.

⚠️ Server-side p99 can look excellent while users on 4G phones wait five seconds. Measure at the edge you actually serve.

10. Cost as an observability signal

Track cost per request, per tenant, and per feature, and alert on anomalies. A 10× cost spike is usually a bug (a retry storm, an unbounded query, a runaway agent loop, a cache that stopped working) and cost is often the fastest detector of it. FinOps and reliability are the same discipline viewed from different angles.

11. Checklist & self-test

Observability readiness

  • Structured logs with consistent field names across services
  • Correlation/trace id in every log, span, message, and error response
  • RED metrics per service; USE metrics per resource; business metrics on the funnel
  • Metric label cardinality bounded — no IDs in labels
  • Distributed tracing including async/queue boundaries
  • Deployment and config-change events overlaid on dashboards
  • SLOs defined with error budgets; multi-window burn-rate alerts
  • Every alert is actionable, owned, and has a runbook
  • Dashboards: service, business, deep-dive
  • Continuous profiling enabled
  • Log volume and telemetry cost reviewed and controlled
  • PII redacted from logs, traces, and error messages
  • Frontend RUM and Core Web Vitals
  • Load test in CI or scheduled, with SLO thresholds as pass/fail

🔍 Questions to test yourself

  • Monitoring vs observability? Monitoring is predefined questions on predefined signals; observability is having enough high-cardinality context to answer new questions without shipping new code.
  • Why not alert on CPU? It's a cause, not a symptom. High CPU with happy users isn't an incident; failing users with normal CPU is. Alert on user-facing SLIs and burn rate.
  • Why percentiles and not averages? Averages hide the tail; users experience the tail. And p99 of a dependency becomes the common case for a request that fans out to it many times.
  • What is cardinality and why does it matter? Each unique label combination is a time series; unbounded labels (user id, raw URL) multiply storage and query cost until the system falls over.
  • How would you debug a latency regression? Metrics to confirm and scope it → change events to find what shipped → traces to locate the span that grew → logs for that trace → profile if it's CPU/memory. Then add a regression guard.
  • How do you set an SLO? From what users need and what the business will pay for, expressed as an SLI you can actually measure, with an error-budget policy that says what happens when it's exhausted.
  • What's the first thing you check in an incident? What changed — deploys, config, feature flags, upstream dependencies. Then blast radius. Mitigate before diagnosing.
